verdict: Same outcome as round 1 and as all four with/without iterations: the specific rule the NEW skill adds is a PRECISION improvement, not a RECALL one. The OLD skill's generic anti-pattern §7 ('don't import from another module') plus the model's own reasoning generalised straight to 'a type import is the same coupling' — so the OLD run caught the violation, just labelled it §7 and skipped the compiles-away/arch:check-blind-spot nuance. Controls even at 3/3 both sides, 0 false positives either side.
why_no_recall_gap: A cross-module `import type` is transparently an instance of 'don't import from another module', which the OLD skill already states. There is no reasoning leap for the model to miss. A rule only produces a recall gap when (a) there is NO general principle in the base skill that subsumes it, or (b) the case actively looks fine under the base skill's framing. `import type` fails both — §7 subsumes it and it looks like exactly what §7 forbids.
what_would_produce_a_recall_gap: A rule with no parent principle in the base skill — e.g. a repo-specific invariant like 'a job body must be a service method, never inline in JobRunner' or 'INJECTION_GUARD is never made conditional' — where the base skill genuinely says nothing and the model has no way to infer it.

A case that looks correct under the base skill — e.g. code that passes every stated rule but violates an unstated one; the base-skill reviewer concludes 'clean' and the new-skill reviewer catches the one thing.

Restricting the baseline: run the OLD-skill agent with NO access to the real repo (cold review). Then it cannot read `.dependency-cruiser.cjs` / sibling modules / the container comments that let it generalise. This is the honest test of what the skill body alone carries — and the scenario where skill content matters most.
